questions.question: The Indicator said the 10 biggest companies are now about 40% of the S&P 500's value, up from 16% ten years ago. What does that mean for someone who owns an S&P 500 index fund?
options: Their money is spread evenly across 500 companies
A big move in a few giant companies now moves their fund a lot more
The fund now only holds 10 companies
The fund has become less risky than ten years ago
questions.explanation: An S&P 500 fund is weighted by company size, so the biggest companies count the most. With the top 10 at 40%, a fall in one giant like Nvidia drags the whole fund down more than it used to. This is market concentration.

questions.question: OpenAI's quarterly revenue reached about $10 billion, yet it is still losing money. How can both be true?
options: Revenue counts money coming in; profit is what's left after costs, and its costs are even higher
Revenue is only counted after a company is profitable
Losses mean revenue fell from the last quarter
Private companies don't have to report revenue
questions.explanation: Revenue is everything customers pay; profit (or loss) is revenue minus all costs. OpenAI spends heavily on computing power, so its costs exceed its $10 billion of sales, while Anthropic reported $17 billion with much smaller losses.

questions.question: After hot October inflation, the two-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.78% and the odds of a December Fed rate hike rose to about 86%. Why would rising inflation make a rate hike more likely?
options: The Fed raises rates to make borrowing cheaper so prices fall
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which cools spending and slows price rises
The Fed must raise rates whenever stocks fall
Rate hikes increase the amount of money in the economy
questions.explanation: When prices rise too fast, the Fed can raise interest rates so loans cost more; people and companies then spend less, which eases inflation. The two-year Treasury yield rises when markets expect that, as it did here.
